title: SLO-led buying guide: platform-ops cheat sheet
body:
Purpose
This is a compact, operational-facing buying guide for platform and infra procurement teams to use when evaluating and negotiating dedicated inference capacity. It frames asks as SLOs and runbook requirements rather than product features, with concrete acceptance tests, fallbacks, and legal-friendly clause language for inclusion in RFPs/SLAs.

Audience
- Platform engineering leads
- Procurement and vendor management
- Security/compliance reviewers (high level)
- Solution architects drafting SOWs

Positioning summary (one-liners to use in decks or calls)
- For platform teams who need predictable token throughput, ask for SLOs not promises: define p95/p99 token latency at target sustained QPS and make it the contract anchor.
- Isolation is operational: demand both logical isolation guarantees and measurable noisy-neighbor controls (priority preemption, eviction policies, telemetry).
- Make procurement decisions on measurable acceptance tests (load envelopes + fidelity checks) and credit/penalty ladders—not vague uptime percentages.

Core SLO constructs (to write into contracts)
1) Predictable throughput SLOs (throughput + latency pairing):
   - Sustained throughput: provider guarantees X tokens/s (or Y inferences/s) sustained over a rolling 1h window per reserved unit with <= Z% degradation (example: 250k tokens/min per 8xA100-equivalent pool with <=10% variance).
   - Tail latency: p95 <= A ms and p99 <= B ms for a defined request profile (e.g., 1k-token generation with 512 context warm).
   - Startup ramp: max warm-up time (time-to-steady-state) after a cold spin <= T seconds under normal autoscale conditions.

2) Availability vs performance SLAs:
   - Separate 'availability' (control-plane/API reachability) from 'performance' (per-token latency and throughput). Contract both.
   - Define scheduled maintenance windows and acceptable rollouts (canary size, rollback policy).

3) Isolation & noisy-neighbor guarantees:
   - Logical isolation: dedicated pools must not share GPUs with other tenants unless explicitly allowed in writing.
   - Noisy-neighbor mitigation: provider must implement QoS (priority classes), cgroup limits or equivalent, and provide telemetry proving enforcement.
   - Eviction policy: define eviction order, notification lead time, and compensating credits if eviction impacts production traffic.

4) Capacity elasticity and burst rules: 
   - Baseline capacity: reserved units guaranteed with linear scaling math documented in contract.
   - Burst allowances: defined burst headroom for sudden spikes (e.g., up to 2x baseline for 10 minutes per hour), with predictable throttling behavior after headroom exhausted.

5) Fault isolation and graceful degradation: 
   - Multi-tier fallback: describe exact fallback behavior when capacity is constrained (e.g., automatically route to pinned lower-capacity model variant, degrade max tokens, or enqueue with backpressure). Require provider to publish fallback latencies under test.

Acceptance tests (operational, vendor-run, and buyer-verified)
- Benchmark harness: require vendor to run a standard harness (we provide) against reserved capacity and publish raw traces. Harness includes:
  - 10m sustained run at 80% of guaranteed QPS
  - 3 1m 2x bursts separated by 10m rest
  - p50/p95/p99 latency histograms and tail token cost breakdown
- Data fidelity test: validate output quality by running a small eval set to ensure quantization/variant changes didn't regress critical prompts.
- Chaos/eviction test: vendor simulates a noisy-tenant event and demonstrates that platform's isolation and eviction policy keep baseline pool within SLOs.

Procurement-friendly clause language (examples to hand to legal)
- Performance SLA: "Provider guarantees sustained throughput of X tokens/sec for the Reserved Pool. If measured throughput falls below 90% of X in any 1-hour rolling window, Customer is eligible for service credits equal to Y% of the monthly reserved fee for each failing hour, up to a cap of Z%."
- Latency SLA: "Provider guarantees p95 latency <= A ms and p99 latency <= B ms based on the agreed request profile. Failure to meet either percentile in two or more non-overlapping hourly windows in a billing month constitutes a breach for credit calculation."
- Isolation covenant: "Reserved Pool hardware will be logically isolated from non-Customer tenants. Provider shall not colocate unrelated Customer workloads to the same GPU instances without explicit written consent. Breach entitles Customer to remediation credits and a 30-day cure period."
- Acceptance test clause: "Upon onboarding, Provider will execute the agreed benchmark harness. Failure to meet acceptance thresholds allows Customer to reject deployed capacity until remediation and a successful retest."

Negotiation tactics and levers (practical playbook)
- Anchor on measurable metrics: insist on percentiles, test harness, and telemetry export (sampled traces, token-level cost breakdown).
- Trade concessions for commitments: if the vendor resists strict credits, accept staged commitments (e.g., commit to 6mo pricing for tighter latency SLOs).
- Ask for operational runway: include a clause requiring the vendor to provide a minimum notice period before any capacity reallocation or major kernel/quantization change (e.g., 30–60 days) with a compatibility test run.
- Right to audit: for enterprise deals, push for an annual or quarterly review where the vendor shares anonymized telemetry and tuning notes.
- Offer migration path: require transferable credits or migration assistance if vendor cannot remediate within SLA windows.

Competitive notes (quick signal capture for buyer teams)
- Vendors who price purely on 'guaranteed vCPU/GPU' often hide variability in per-token performance—so translate vendor claims into SLOs and run the harness.
- Cloud-managed endpoints sometimes have faster time-to-scale but lower isolation; validate noisy-neighbor guardrails.
- Some vendors offer "soft isolation" (scheduling preferences) vs "hard isolation" (dedicated hardware). Hard isolation reduces noisy neighbor risk but costs more—map this to cost of downtime for your product.

Elevator scripts (for internal champions to use)
- For platform leads: "We need supplier SLAs that map directly to our incident budget. I want p99 and sustained throughput guarantees, plus an acceptance test we can run before cutover. Without that, we carry hidden risk in production."
- For procurement: "We are buying predictability. Tie credits to measurable performance metrics, not just uptime percentages — that protects our API SLAs and downstream product SLAs."
- For finance/CFO: "This is about OPEX predictability: we trade a slightly higher reservation price for lower variance in cost and lower operational risk from outages or throttling."

Operational checklist (what to request during sales cycles)
- Benchmark harness artifact and vendor-run report
- Telemetry exports (sampled traces, capacity utilization, per-route latency)
- Onboarding runbook with acceptance test steps and timeline
- Eviction and maintenance policy doc
- SLA template with credit ladder and remediation timelines
- Migration and decommissioning assistance commitment

Open questions to clarify with providers
- How are kernel/quantization upgrades handled and communicated?
- What is the eviction priority logic under pressure?
- Can we get a read-only telemetry stream into our observability stack?
- Where are customer pools physically located and how is regional failover handled?

Example negotiation timeline (recommended cadence)
1) Discovery + ask list (week 0): deliver SLO list, acceptance harness, and desired credits ladder.
2) Vendor counter (week 1): vendor returns feasibility notes and proposed SLO numbers.
3) Technical validation (week 2–3): run vendor harness in a shadow environment, share results.
4) Legal redlines + final SLOs (week 3–4): incorporate acceptance clause and credits.
5) Onboard + acceptance test (week 4–6): vendor executes harness, buyer verifies.

Appendix: sample SLOs (copy/paste into RFP)
- Sustained throughput: 150k tokens/min per reserved unit, measured over rolling 1-hour windows, tolerance +/-10%.
- p95 latency: <= 280ms for 512-token eval profile; p99 latency: <= 950ms.
- Warm start time: <= 90s to reach steady-state from cold start for a single pool node.
- Burst policy: up to 2x baseline for at most 10 minutes per 60-minute period, then linear throttling.

Next steps (for GTM and field)
- Validate this playbook against two recent RFIs to capture vendor pushback and tighten legal language.
- Build a short one-pager for sales engineers summarizing the top 3 SLO asks and the acceptance test.
- Add a standard harness to our public repo and ship sample artifacts for procurement teams to use in negotiations.

Notes & provenance
- Drafted from combined feedback from platform customers, solutions engineering pilots, and recent procurement negotiations.
- This is intentionally vendor-agnostic and ops-first: language should be adapted by legal and platform teams for specific deals.
